about.title: About James Wolfe
about.body:
James writes on grace, patience, and the ordinary shape of the Christian life. He lives with his family and is currently working on his first book.

## Mission

This site exists to help weary Christians find comfort and confidence in Christ — through writing that takes the ordinary, undramatic parts of faith seriously.

## Currently

Writing weekly, working on a first book, and slowly building out a public archive of quotations that have shaped his thinking.

articles.title: On the Patience of God
articles.excerpt: There is a particular kind of shame that visits us not when we fail, but when we fail again — the same sin, the same excuse, the same quiet apology whispered for the hundredth time. I used to think God's patience had a bottom. I am learning, slowly, that it does not.
articles.body:
There is a particular kind of shame that visits us not when we fail, but when we fail again — the same sin, the same excuse, the same quiet apology whispered for the hundredth time. I used to think God's patience had a bottom. I am learning, slowly, that it does not.

We tend to imagine patience as a kind of reluctant tolerance — a parent counting silently to ten, a teacher exhaling before the fifteenth interruption. But that isn't quite what Scripture means when it describes the patience of God. His patience is not gritted teeth. It is settled purpose.

:::scripture 2 Peter 3:9
The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
:::

Notice what the patience is *for*. It isn't aimless forbearance. It is aimed at repentance — at bringing us, unhurried but unrelenting, to the place where we finally stop running. That distinction matters more than it first appears. A patience with no direction is just delay. A patience with a purpose is closer to love holding its ground.

## The Danger of Presuming on It

Paul warns the Romans about a subtler danger than despair — the danger of presuming on God's kindness as though it were indifference.

:::scripture Romans 2:4
Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
:::

I have been on both sides of this. There are seasons where I have treated God's patience as a locked door I was too ashamed to knock on, and seasons where I have treated it as a door that would simply never close, no matter how long I stayed away. Both are a misreading. His patience is neither a wall nor a blank check. It is an invitation, open for exactly as long as he decides — which, mercifully, has so far always been long enough.

I don't know how to end an article like this except plainly: if you are waiting to feel worthy of coming back before you come back, you have the order backward. The patience is not the reward for arriving. It is the reason you're able to.

articles.title: The Ordinary Tuesday
articles.excerpt: Most of my sanctification has not happened on mountaintops. It has happened in the dishes, in the traffic, in the eleventh phone call from a friend in crisis when I had nothing left to give. I am starting to suspect that this — the unremarkable middle of the week — is where most of the Christian life actually takes place.

articles.title: What the Psalms Taught Me About Complaint
articles.excerpt: For years I thought lament was a failure of faith — a crack in the foundation that a stronger Christian wouldn't need. Then I read the Psalms honestly for the first time and realized how much of Israel's worship was, quite plainly, complaint addressed to God rather than about him.

articles.title: A Slower Kind of Faithfulness
articles.excerpt: We have built a culture that rewards the dramatic testimony and quietly ignores the fifty-year marriage, the unremarkable deacon, the Sunday school teacher nobody wrote a book about. I want to make a case for the long, undramatic obedience that most of us are actually called to.
